title: Metaphor, examples and analogy
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Haili Hughes opens with two classroom misfires, her own Tony Blair example and an observed lesson using David Beckham to explain Macbeth, to show that out-of-date analogies sink rather than anchor understanding. Drawing on Kuleshova and colleagues' account of analogy as shared relational structure, she argues that good analogies help pupils see how something works, but they are selective, highlighting some features and hiding others. Because novices notice surface resemblance before deep structure, teachers must manage analogies rather than simply produce clever comparisons. She sets out three implications: the source must be genuinely familiar to pupils, the mapping must be made explicit, and the point where the analogy breaks down must be spelled out. She extends the argument to metaphor as a fundamental feature of thought embedded in subject language, warns that poor analogies create an illusion of understanding, and treats analogies as temporary scaffolds. Finally she links analogy to transfer and schema-building, concluding that disciplined use of explanation is part of the ordinary craft of teaching.
points: Analogies work through shared relational structure rather than surface similarity, so their value lies in helping pupils see how something works, not in vividness.
Three practical rules follow: use a source pupils genuinely know, name the mapping explicitly, and state where the analogy stops working, which also doubles as a check for understanding.
A poor analogy can give pupils the feeling of understanding without the reality, surviving until the first half-decent question exposes that they remembered the image and not the concept.
Subject vocabulary such as current, genetic code or functions as machines is itself metaphorical and carries hidden assumptions, so teachers are always using metaphor whether or not they notice.
Analogy is tied to transfer: the aim is for pupils to recognise shared structure between problems whose surface details differ, one of the hardest and most important things to teach.
quotes: Yet, it is fair to say that good teachers make the unfamiliar familiar and used carefully, examples, metaphor and analogy can help pupils grasp difficult ideas, notice underlying structure and begin to transfer knowledge. Used badly, as illustrated above, they can leave behind a tidy misunderstanding.
Yet explanation is hard because expertise distorts our sense of difficulty. Once you know something well, it becomes difficult to remember what it feels like not to know it.
This is the problem with lazy praise of analogies. They are not automatically clarifying. They are selective.

An analogy drawn from cricket, mortgages, cassette tapes or sailing may seem wonderfully clear to the adult in the room and mean next to nothing to a thirteen-year-old. An analogy only helps if pupils already understand the thing being used to explain the new idea.
Good explanations do not merely offer a bridge. They also put railings on it. Pupils need to know the limits of the comparison.
Teachers ignore that at their peril. We are always using metaphor, whether we notice it or not. The real choice is not whether to use metaphor, but whether to use it carelessly or well.
Of course, there is a risk here. A poor analogy can give pupils the feeling of understanding without the reality of it. The explanation sounds clear, the nodding begins and the teacher moves on.
